ety.text: From Middle English fom, foom, from Old English fām, from Proto-West Germanic *faim, from Proto-Germanic *faimaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)poHy-m-os, from *(s)poH(y)- (“foam”). Cognate with German Feim (“foam”), Latin spūma (“foam”), Latin pūmex (“pumice”), Sanskrit फेन (phéna, “foam”), possibly Northern Kurdish fê (“epilepsy”).

senses.d: A substance composed of a large collection of bubbles or their solidified remains, especially
A collection of small bubbles created when the surface of a body of water is moved by tides, wind, etc.
ex: ’Tis thou that rigg’st the bark and plough’st the foam,
And the heaven became livid with the violence of the tempest […] and the river was tormented into foam […]

senses.d: A collection of small bubbles formed from bodily fluids such as saliva or sweat.
ex: “Again. Tell it again!” cried Fagin, tightening his grasp on Sikes, and brandishing his other hand aloft as the foam flew from his lips.
The horses were flecked with foam and their breathing was noisy.

senses.d: A collection of small bubbles on the surface of a liquid that is heated, fermented or carbonated.
ex: a quart jug with a crown of foam upon it
The last of the milk vanished in a swirl of foam and gurgling.

senses.d: A collection of small bubbles created by mixing soap with water.
ex: […] she concentrated on the foam in the sink, tempering the water.
Later we shared a bath with foam up to our ears, like they always discreetly have in films.

senses.d: A collection of small bubbles formed by mixing an extinguishing agent with water, used to cover and extinguish fires.
A food prepared in the form of a mass of airy bubbles.
ex: His specialty is a mango foam.

senses.d: A material formed by trapping pockets of gas in a liquid or solid.
ex: A foam mat can soften a hard seat.
He is in Europe, across the foam.
How slowly does sad Time his feathers moue? / Hast thee O fayrest Planet to thy home / Within the Westerne fome:

When the fierce North-wind with his airy forces
Rears up the Baltic to a foaming fury;
They were both silent for a measure of moments, and then Syme's speech came with a rush, like the sudden foaming of champagne.

senses.d: To spew saliva as foam; to foam at the mouth.
To coat or cover with foam.
ex: It used to be common practice to foam the runway prior to an emergency landing, in case a fuel-fed fire occurred.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French écume, escume, from Old French escume (“froth, foam”), from Frankish *skūm (“froth, foam”), possibly via Vulgar Latin *scūma (compare Medieval Latin scuma), from Proto-Germanic *skūmaz (“foam”).

Inherited from Old French mosse (“moss”), from Frankish *mosa (“moss”), from Proto-Germanic *musą (“moss”). For the culinary sense one might suspect influence by Dutch moes, German Mus (both “mush, purée”).
Via Late Latin schuma from Old High German scum (modern German Schaum). Compare Piedmontese and Sicilian scuma.
Inherited from Old Spanish espuma, from Latin spūma.
